Describes future events, intentions, and predictions.
Expresses an action that will have been completed before another future action or specified time.
Expresses an action completed prior to another past action.

grammar_rules.title: Formation of regular -er verbs in the present tense
grammar_rules.summary: Drop -er from the infinitive and add endings: -e, -es, -e, -ons, -ez, -ent.
grammar_rules.explanation: To conjugate a regular -er verb in the present tense, remove the infinitive ending -er to find the stem, then add the endings corresponding to the subject pronoun.
exceptions: aller is irregular
spelling/stem changing -er verbs have minor adjustments
notes: The endings -e, -es, and -ent are all silent in spoken French.

common_mistakes.explanation: The 3rd person plural ending -ent is completely silent.

grammar_rules.title: Spelling change in verbs ending in -ger
grammar_rules.summary: Keep the 'e' before -ons in the 'nous' form to preserve the soft 'g' sound (mangeons).
grammar_rules.explanation: For verbs ending in -ger (like manger, voyager, nager, partager), add an 'e' before the -ons ending of nous (nous mangeons, nous voyageons) to keep the soft 'g' sound.

steps: In the nous form, retain 'e' after 'g' before 'ons'

notes: Only the nous form is affected in the present tense.

common_mistakes.explanation: Without 'e', 'g' would sound hard as in 'gant'.

grammar_rules.title: Spelling change in verbs ending in -cer
grammar_rules.summary: Change 'c' to 'ç' before -ons in the 'nous' form to preserve the soft 's' sound (commençons).
grammar_rules.explanation: For verbs ending in -cer (like commencer, avancer, lancer, remplacer), change 'c' to 'ç' before the 'o' in nous (nous commençons) to keep the soft 's' sound.

steps: In the nous form, change 'c' to 'ç' before 'ons'

notes: Only the nous form is affected in the present tense.

common_mistakes.explanation: Without cedilla, 'c' before 'o' sounds like 'k'.

grammar_rules.title: Stem change in verbs ending in -yer
grammar_rules.summary: The 'y' changes to 'i' in all forms except 'nous' and 'vous' (j'envoie, nous envoyons).
grammar_rules.explanation: In verbs ending in -oyer and -uyer (envoyer, nettoyer, essuyer), 'y' changes to 'i' before a silent 'e' (boot pattern: je, tu, il, ils). For -ayer verbs (payer), both 'i' and 'y' forms are accepted (je paie / je paye).

steps: Change 'y' to 'i' in singular and 3rd person plural forms
Keep 'y' in nous and vous forms

exceptions: payer allows both je paie and je paye

grammar_rules.title: Stem change in verbs with -e- + consonant + -er
grammar_rules.summary: The silent 'e' changes to 'è' in all forms except 'nous' and 'vous' (j'achète, nous achetons).
grammar_rules.explanation: Verbs like acheter, emmener, lever, peser add a grave accent (è) in the boot forms (je, tu, il, ils) where the ending is silent.

steps: Add accent grave 'è' to stem in je, tu, il, ils
Keep unaccented 'e' in nous and vous

common_mistakes.explanation: Nous and vous keep the unaccented stem.

grammar_rules.title: Stem change in verbs with -é- + consonant + -er
grammar_rules.summary: The 'é' changes to 'è' in all forms except 'nous' and 'vous' (je répète, nous répétons).
grammar_rules.explanation: Verbs like répéter, célébrer, espérer, préférer change the acute accent (é) to a grave accent (è) in the boot forms.

steps: Change 'é' to 'è' in je, tu, il, ils

grammar_rules.title: Verbs ending in -eler and -eter doubling consonant
grammar_rules.summary: Verbs like appeler and jeter double the 'l' or 't' before silent endings (j'appelle, je jette).
grammar_rules.explanation: Verbs like appeler, rappeler, renouveler, épeler double the 'l' (ll) in boot forms. Verbs like jeter double the 't' (tt). Nous and vous keep a single consonant.

steps: Double 'l' or 't' in je, tu, il, ils
Single 'l' or 't' in nous and vous

exceptions: geler and acheter take accent grave instead of doubling consonant

common_mistakes.explanation: Nous and vous have single 'l'.

grammar_rules.title: Present tense for general statements and ongoing actions
grammar_rules.summary: French present translates simple present, present continuous, and emphatic present in English.
grammar_rules.explanation: In French, 'Valérie parle' translates to 'Valérie speaks', 'Valérie is speaking', and 'Valérie does speak'. There is no separate progressive form with 'être' unless using the construction 'être en train de'.
notes: Do not say 'elle est parlant' for 'she is speaking'.

common_mistakes.explanation: French does not use être + present participle for ongoing actions.

grammar_rules.title: Present tense expressing near future
grammar_rules.summary: The present tense can express an action planned or happening in the near future.
grammar_rules.explanation: Just as in English, a present tense verb combined with a future time marker indicates planned future action: 'Il part demain soir' (He is leaving tomorrow evening).
usage_conditions: Planned upcoming events with time adverbs

grammar_rules.title: Present tense for habitual actions
grammar_rules.summary: Describes habits, routines, and repeated actions in the present.
grammar_rules.explanation: Use the present tense with frequency markers like 'tous les jours', 'd'habitude', 'toujours' to describe habitual events.

grammar_rules.title: Historical and dramatic present
grammar_rules.summary: Used to recount historical facts or past events with dramatic immediacy.
grammar_rules.explanation: In narratives and history, the present tense makes past events feel vivid and immediate: 'Flaubert publie Madame Bovary et c'est le scandale!'.

grammar_rules.title: Continuous action with être en train de + infinitive
grammar_rules.summary: Expresses that an action is currently in progress ('in the middle of doing something').
grammar_rules.explanation: To explicitly emphasize that an action is in progress at this exact moment, use conjugated être + en train de + infinitive: 'Je suis en train de parler' (I am in the middle of talking).

steps: Add 'en train de' (or 'en train d'' before vowel)

notes: Use 'd'' before vowel or silent h (en train d'étudier).

common_mistakes.correct: Je suis en train de parler
common_mistakes.explanation: Use être en train de + infinitive, not present participle.

grammar_rules.title: Action continuing into the present with depuis, il y a... que, ça fait... que
grammar_rules.summary: Use the French present tense with 'depuis' for actions that began in the past and continue in the present.
grammar_rules.explanation: Unlike English which uses the present perfect ('I have been living here for three years'), French uses the PRESENT tense with 'depuis': 'J'habite à Nice depuis trois ans'. Questions use 'depuis quand' (since when) or 'depuis combien de temps' (for how long).

patterns: [VERBE AU PRÉSENT] + depuis + [DURÉE / POINT DE DÉPART]

usage_conditions: Ongoing action initiated in the past
notes: If the action is completed and no longer continues, use passé composé + pendant/il y a, not depuis.

common_mistakes.wrong: J'ai habité ici depuis trois ans (when still living there)
common_mistakes.explanation: In French, use the present tense if the action is still ongoing.

grammar_rules.title: Regular -ir verbs (finir type) in the present tense
grammar_rules.summary: Drop -ir and add -is, -is, -it, -issons, -issez, -issent (with -iss- infix in plural).
grammar_rules.explanation: Regular 2nd group verbs (finir, choisir, remplir, réussir, obéir) take endings -is, -is, -it in singular, and insert -iss- before plural endings: -issons, -issez, -issent.
exceptions: Irregular short -ir verbs (partir, sortir) do not take -iss-

grammar_rules.title: Irregular short -ir verbs (partir, sortir, dormir type)
grammar_rules.summary: Singular stem drops the final consonant: je pars, tu pars, il part; plural stem keeps it: nous partons, vous partez, ils partent.
grammar_rules.explanation: Verbs like partir (je pars, nous partons), sortir (je sors, nous sortons), dormir (je dors, nous dormons), servir (je sers, nous servons), sentir (je sens, nous sentons), mentir (je mens, nous mentons) drop the final consonant of the root in the singular and restore it in the plural.

grammar_rules.title: Regular -re verbs (vendre type) in the present tense
grammar_rules.summary: Drop -re and add -s, -s, - (nothing / keeps d), -ons, -ez, -ent.
grammar_rules.explanation: Regular -re verbs (vendre, attendre, descendre, entendre, perdre, rendre, répondre) add -s, -s, nothing in the 3rd person singular (il vend), and -ons, -ez, -ent in plural.
exceptions: prendre group, mettre, battre, etc. have different patterns
notes: Note that il/elle/on has NO ending added; it simply ends in the stem 'd' (il vend, elle attend).

common_mistakes.explanation: No 't' is added to 3rd person singular when stem ends in d.

grammar_rules.title: Conjugation of prendre and its compounds in the present tense
grammar_rules.summary: Prendre drops 'd' in nous/vous (prenons, prenez) and doubles 'n' in ils (prennent).
grammar_rules.explanation: Verbs of the prendre family (prendre, apprendre, comprendre, surprendre, entreprendre) conjugate: je prends, tu prends, il prend, nous prenons, vous prenez, ils prennent.

patterns: prends, prends, prend, prenons, prenez, prennent

common_mistakes.explanation: Double 'n' in ils/elles prennent.

grammar_rules.title: Three ways to ask a question in French
grammar_rules.summary: Questions can be formed by intonation (informal), 'est-ce que' (standard), or subject-verb inversion (formal).
grammar_rules.explanation:
1. Intonation: Tu parles français? (voice rises at end)
2. Est-ce que: Est-ce que tu parles français?
3. Inversion: Parles-tu français?
usage_conditions: Spoken informal, standard, and formal writing
notes: Add '-t-' in inversion when 3rd person singular verb ends in a vowel before il/elle/on: Parle-t-il? Aime-t-elle?

common_mistakes.explanation: Insert euphonic -t- between two vowel sounds in inversion.

grammar_rules.title: Basic negation with ne ... pas
grammar_rules.summary: Place 'ne' before the conjugated verb and 'pas' after it (n' before vowels).
grammar_rules.explanation: To make a sentence negative, place 'ne' (or 'n'') before the conjugated verb and 'pas' directly after: 'Il ne parle pas anglais'. In compound tenses, 'pas' precedes the past participle: 'Il n'a pas parlé'.

steps: Place ne / n' before conjugated verb

notes: Indefinite and partitive articles (un, une, des, du, de la) change to 'de / d'' in a direct negative, except with être.

common_mistakes.wrong: Je ne veux pas du vin
common_mistakes.correct: Je ne veux pas de vin
common_mistakes.explanation: Partitive changes to 'de' in negation.

grammar_rules.title: Negative adverbs: ne... jamais, ne... plus, ne... rien, ne... personne
grammar_rules.summary: Replace 'pas' with 'jamais' (never), 'plus' (no more/longer), 'rien' (nothing), 'personne' (nobody).
grammar_rules.explanation:
- ne... jamais: never
- ne... plus: no longer, not anymore
- ne... rien: nothing
- ne... personne: nobody / no one
Note: 'personne' follows the past participle in compound tenses (Je n'ai vu personne), whereas 'rien', 'plus', 'jamais' precede it (Je n'ai rien vu).

steps: Place negative word in place of pas

notes: Never combine 'pas' with 'jamais', 'plus', or 'rien' in standard French.

common_mistakes.explanation: Do not use 'pas' with 'rien'.

grammar_rules.title: Conjugation and uses of être (to be) in the present
grammar_rules.summary: Irregular: je suis, tu es, il/elle/on est, nous sommes, vous êtes, ils/elles sont.
grammar_rules.explanation: Être is one of the two core auxiliary verbs in French. Used for identity, nationality, profession, adjectives, location, and passive voice.

steps: je suis, tu es, il est, nous sommes, vous êtes, ils sont

notes: Do not use articles with profession after être: 'Il est médecin' (not 'Il est un médecin').

common_mistakes.explanation: Omit article with unmodified professions after être.

grammar_rules.title: Distinction between c'est and il est
grammar_rules.summary: Use 'c'est' before modified nouns, proper names, pronouns, and general superlative comments; use 'il/elle est' before bare adjectives, professions, and nationalities.
grammar_rules.explanation:
Use c'est + noun phrase (C'est un bon médecin), c'est + pronoun (C'est moi), c'est + proper noun (C'est Marie).
Use il/elle est + adjective alone (Il est intelligent), il/elle est + bare profession (Il est médecin).
usage_conditions: Identifying persons or things vs describing specific qualities

common_mistakes.explanation: Use c'est when the noun is modified by an article.

grammar_rules.title: Conjugation of avoir (to have) in the present
grammar_rules.summary: Irregular: j'ai, tu as, il/elle/on a, nous avons, vous avez, ils/elles ont.
grammar_rules.explanation: Avoir is used to express possession, age, and forms many essential idiomatic physical/mental states where English uses 'to be'.

steps: j'ai, tu as, il a, nous avons, vous avez, ils ont

notes: Notice liaison in nous avons [nuzavõ], vous avez [vuzave], ils ont [ilzõ].

common_mistakes.explanation: French uses avoir for age.

grammar_rules.title: Idiomatic expressions with avoir
grammar_rules.summary: French uses avoir + noun where English uses to be + adjective (avoir faim, avoir peur, avoir raison, etc.).
grammar_rules.explanation:
Essential expressions:
- avoir faim (to be hungry)
- avoir soif (to be thirsty)
- avoir chaud / froid (to be hot / cold)
- avoir peur de (to be afraid of)
- avoir raison / tort (to be right / wrong)
- avoir honte de (to be ashamed of)
- avoir sommeil (to be sleepy)
- avoir besoin de (to need)
- avoir envie de (to feel like / desire)
- avoir l'air (to look / seem)
- avoir l'habitude de (to be used to)

common_mistakes.explanation: Use avoir for hungry/thirsty/hot/cold.

grammar_rules.title: Difference between savoir and connaître (to know)
grammar_rules.summary: Savoir = to know facts, information, or how to do something (+ infinitive/clause); Connaître = to be acquainted with people, places, or things (+ direct object).
grammar_rules.explanation:
- Savoir (je sais, tu sais, il sait, nous savons, vous savez, ils savent): followed by a clause (que, où, quand, pourquoi) or an infinitive (savoir nager).
- Connaître (je connais, tu connais, il connaît, nous connaissons, vous connaissez, ils connaissent): followed directly by a noun (connaître Paris, connaître quelqu'un). Never followed by a verb or que clause.
usage_conditions: Knowing facts/skills vs familiarity with persons/places
restrictions: Connaître is never followed by an infinitive or que clause.

common_mistakes.explanation: Use savoir before infinitive for knowing how to do something.

grammar_rules.title: Conjugation of aller (to go) in the present
grammar_rules.summary: Irregular: je vais, tu vas, il/elle/on va, nous allons, vous allez, ils/elles vont.
grammar_rules.explanation: Aller is an irregular 3rd group verb despite its -er ending. It is used for movement and forming the immediate future (futur proche).

steps: je vais, tu vas, il va, nous allons, vous allez, ils vont

common_mistakes.explanation: 3rd person plural is vont.

grammar_rules.title: The immediate future (futur proche): aller + infinitive
grammar_rules.summary: Conjugated aller in present + infinitive of action verb expresses 'going to do something'.
grammar_rules.explanation: Formed with the present tense of aller followed by the infinitive: 'Je vais partir' (I am going to leave). In the negative, ne... pas surrounds aller: 'Je ne vais pas partir'.
notes: Very frequent in spoken French.

grammar_rules.title: Conjugation of venir (to come) in the present
grammar_rules.summary: Irregular: je viens, tu viens, il/elle/on vient, nous venons, vous venez, ils/elles viennent.
grammar_rules.explanation: Venir and tenir (and all their compounds: devenir, revenir, prévenir, maintenir, retenir) follow the same conjugation pattern.

steps: viens, viens, vient, venons, venez, viennent

common_mistakes.explanation: Double 'n' and 'ie' stem in 3rd plural.

grammar_rules.title: The immediate past (passé récent): venir de + infinitive
grammar_rules.summary: Conjugated venir in present + de + infinitive expresses 'having just done something'.
grammar_rules.explanation: Use venir in the present followed by 'de' (or 'd'') and the infinitive of the verb to express an action that just happened: 'Je viens de manger' (I just ate / I have just eaten).

common_mistakes.wrong: Je viens manger (meaning I just ate)
common_mistakes.explanation: Without 'de', it means 'I am coming to eat'.

grammar_rules.title: Conjugation of faire (to do, to make) in the present
grammar_rules.summary: Irregular: je fais, tu fais, il/elle/on fait, nous faisons, vous faites, ils/elles font.
grammar_rules.explanation: Notice the irregular 2nd person plural 'vous faites' and 3rd person plural 'ils font', and the pronunciation of 'nous faisons' [nufəzõ].

steps: je fais, tu fais, il fait, nous faisons, vous faites, ils font

notes: One of only three verbs taking -tes with vous (être -> vous êtes, faire -> vous faites, dire -> vous dites).

common_mistakes.explanation: Vous form is irregular: vous faites.

grammar_rules.title: The causative construction: faire + infinitive
grammar_rules.summary: Conjugated faire + infinitive means 'to have something done' or 'to cause someone to do something'.
grammar_rules.explanation: When you have someone else perform an action or cause an event, use faire + infinitive: 'Je fais réparer ma voiture' (I am having my car repaired); 'Il fait rire ses amis' (He makes his friends laugh).

steps: Follow immediately with infinitive of action verb

notes: Object pronouns precede faire: 'Je la fais réparer'.

common_mistakes.explanation: The infinitive immediately follows faire.

grammar_rules.title: Meanings and nuances of the verb devoir
grammar_rules.summary: Devoir expresses obligation (must/have to), owing money/favors, probability/supposition, and should (conditionnel).
grammar_rules.explanation:
1. Obligation: 'Tu dois partir' (You must leave).
2. Owing: 'Je vous dois dix euros' (I owe you 10 euros).
3. Probability: 'Il doit être midi' (It must be noon / It probably is noon).
4. Advice / Should (in conditional): 'Vous devriez appeler' (You should call).

steps: je dois, tu dois, il doit, nous devons, vous devez, ils doivent

grammar_rules.title: Existential and temporal uses of il y a
grammar_rules.summary: Means 'there is / there are' with nouns; in negation becomes 'il n'y a pas de'; inverted 'y a-t-il?'.
grammar_rules.explanation: Il y a is invariable regardless of whether singular or plural follows: 'Il y a un livre', 'Il y a des livres'. Negative form: 'Il n'y a pas de problème'.
notes: Partitive changes to 'de' in negative: 'Il n'y a pas d'eau'.

common_mistakes.explanation: Il y a never changes to plural.

grammar_rules.title: The impersonal construction il s'agit de
grammar_rules.summary: Translates to 'it is about / it is a matter of / it concerns'. Always uses impersonal subject 'il'.
grammar_rules.explanation: 'Dans ce livre, il s'agit du président' (In this book, it's about the president). In question form: 'De quoi s'agit-il?' (What is it about?).
usage_conditions: Identifying topics, subjects of discussion, critical matters
restrictions: Never use personal subjects (ce livre s'agit de is incorrect; say ce livre parle de or dans ce livre il s'agit de).

common_mistakes.correct: Dans ce film, il s'agit d'une histoire...
common_mistakes.explanation: Il s'agit de is exclusively impersonal.

grammar_rules.title: Conjugation of verbs ending in -eindre and -aindre
grammar_rules.summary: Singular drops 'd' and takes -s, -s, -t (je crains, il craint); plural stem has 'gn' (nous craignons, ils craignent).
grammar_rules.explanation: Verbs like peindre, craindre, plaindre, feindre, éteindre, atteindre conjugate: je peins, tu peins, il peint, nous peignons, vous peignez, ils peignent. Past participle ends in -t: peint, craint, plaint, éteint.

common_mistakes.explanation: Plural stem uses 'gn'.

grammar_rules.title: Reflexive verbs and pronoun placement
grammar_rules.summary: Reflexive pronouns match the subject: je me, tu te, il/elle/on se, nous nous, vous vous, ils/elles se.
grammar_rules.explanation: A reflexive verb indicates that the subject performs an action on itself. Reflexive pronouns (me, te, se, nous, vous, se) precede the conjugated verb in simple tenses.
usage_conditions: Actions done to oneself (daily routine, grooming)
notes: Before a vowel or silent h, me, te, se become m', t', s'.

common_mistakes.explanation: Use reflexive pronoun 'me', not disjunctive pronoun 'moi'.

grammar_rules.title: Reciprocal verbs: actions done to one another
grammar_rules.summary: Used only in the plural persons (nous, vous, ils/elles) to express 'each other' or 'one another'.
grammar_rules.explanation: Verbs like se parler (to speak to each other), se voir (to see each other), s'aimer (to love each other), se téléphoner (to call each other) express reciprocal actions.
usage_conditions: Mutual interactions between two or more people
restrictions: Can only be used with plural subjects (nous, vous, ils, elles).

grammar_rules.title: Passive and idiomatic pronominals
grammar_rules.summary: Pronominal verbs with passive meanings (ça se vend bien) or unique idiomatic meanings (se souvenir, se rendre compte).
grammar_rules.explanation:
1. Passive pronominal: 'Le vin français se vend partout' (French wine is sold everywhere).
2. Idiomatic pronominal: 'se souvenir de' (to remember), 'se rendre compte de' (to realize), 'se dépêcher' (to hurry), 'se tromper' (to make a mistake).

common_mistakes.explanation: Use se rendre compte de for realizing something.

grammar_rules.title: Pronominal pronouns in imperative and with infinitives
grammar_rules.summary: In affirmative imperative, pronouns follow with hyphen and 'te' becomes 'toi' (Lève-toi!). With infinitive, pronoun precedes the infinitive (Je veux me lever).
grammar_rules.explanation:
Affirmative imperative: 'Lève-toi!', 'Habillons-nous!', 'Dépêchez-vous!'.
Negative imperative: 'Ne te lève pas!', 'Ne nous dépêchons pas!'.
With infinitive: Reflexive pronoun always matches the subject of the infinitive: 'Je vais me promener' (not 'Je vais se promener').

common_mistakes.explanation: Reflexive pronoun must agree with subject 'je'.

grammar_rules.title: Formation of regular past participles
grammar_rules.summary: -er verbs -> -é; -ir verbs -> -i; -re verbs -> -u.
grammar_rules.explanation:
Regular verbs form the past participle by changing the infinitive ending:
- parler -> parlé
- finir -> fini
- vendre -> vendu

grammar_rules.title: Formation of the passé composé with avoir
grammar_rules.summary: Present of avoir + past participle. Most verbs use avoir as auxiliary.
grammar_rules.explanation: The vast majority of French verbs use avoir: 'J'ai parlé', 'Tu as fini', 'Nous avons vendu'. In standard word order, the past participle does NOT agree with the subject.

steps: Add past participle of action verb

usage_conditions: Completed specific past actions and events
notes: Adverbs like bien, mal, beaucoup, déjà, trop, vite usually sit between avoir and the past participle: 'J'ai bien mangé'.

common_mistakes.explanation: No agreement with subject when conjugated with avoir.

grammar_rules.title: Agreement of past participle with preceding direct object (P.D.O.)
grammar_rules.summary: When a direct object precedes the verb with avoir, the past participle agrees in gender and number with that direct object.
grammar_rules.explanation:
If the direct object pronoun (le, la, les), relative pronoun (que), or noun in a question with quel/combien precedes avoir, the past participle agrees:
- 'Les fleurs que j'ai achetées' (fem. pl.)
- 'Ces lettres? Je les ai écrites' (fem. pl.)
usage_conditions: Direct object pronoun / que / quel preceding avoir
exceptions: No agreement with indirect object pronouns (lui, leur) or with 'en'.

common_mistakes.explanation: Leur is an indirect object; no agreement.

grammar_rules.title: Verbs conjugated with être in the passé composé (DR & MRS VANDERTRAMP)
grammar_rules.summary: Intransitive movement and state-change verbs take être; the past participle ALWAYS agrees with the subject.
grammar_rules.explanation:
Key verbs taking être:
Devenir, Revenir, Monter, Rester, Sortir, Venir, Aller, Naître, Descendre, Entrer, Rentrer, Tomber, Retourner, Arriver, Mourir, Partir.
The past participle agrees with the subject in gender and number: 'Elle est allée', 'Ils sont partis'.
usage_conditions: Specific intransitive movement and change of state verbs
notes: Pronominal verbs also always use être as auxiliary.

common_mistakes.explanation: Participle must agree in gender and number with subject when conjugated with être.

grammar_rules.title: Verbs conjugated with both avoir and être depending on direct object
grammar_rules.summary: Six verbs (monter, descendre, sortir, rentrer, passer, retourner) take avoir when followed by a direct object, but être when used intransitively.
grammar_rules.explanation:
- Intransitive (movement) -> être: 'Elle est sortie' (She went out).
- Transitive (direct object) -> avoir: 'Elle a sorti la poubelle' (She took out the trash).
- 'Je suis passé chez toi' (I stopped by) vs 'J'ai passé un examen' (I took an exam / spent time).
usage_conditions: Transitive vs intransitive usage of movement verbs

common_mistakes.explanation: Use avoir when a direct object follows.

grammar_rules.title: Formation of the imparfait
grammar_rules.summary: Take the 'nous' present stem and add: -ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient. Only one exception: être (ét-).
grammar_rules.explanation:
Find the stem by dropping -ons from the present tense 'nous' form:
- nous parlons -> parl- + ais/ais/ait/ions/iez/aient
- nous finissons -> finiss- + ais/ais/ait/ions/iez/aient
- nous vendons -> vend- + ais/ais/ait/ions/iez/aient
- Exception: être uses stem 'ét-' (j'étais, tu étais, etc.).
exceptions: être is the only irregular stem: ét-

common_mistakes.explanation: Only être is irregular in the imparfait.

grammar_rules.title: Imparfait versus passé composé
grammar_rules.summary: Passé composé = foreground, specific completed events, interruptions. Imparfait = background, descriptions, ongoing states, habitual actions.
grammar_rules.explanation:
Use Passé Composé for:
1. Completed actions with definite beginning/end
2. Specific number of times or time limits
3. Chain of sequential events
4. Interrupter action

Use Imparfait for:
1. Setting the scene / background description (weather, emotions, physical states)
2. Repeated or habitual actions (used to / would)
3. Ongoing action in progress when another event occurred ('was doing').
notes: Certain verbs shift meaning between tenses: savoir (savait = knew facts; a su = found out), connaître (connaissait = knew; a connu = met for first time), vouloir (voulait = wanted; a voulu = tried / refused).

common_mistakes.wrong: Il pleuvait quand je suis parti vs Il a plu quand je suis parti
common_mistakes.correct: Il pleuvait (background) quand je suis parti (event)
common_mistakes.explanation: Background weather uses imparfait.

grammar_rules.title: Suggestions and wishes with Si on + imparfait
grammar_rules.summary: Starting a sentence with 'Si on' + imparfait expresses a friendly suggestion ('How about...? / What if we...?').
grammar_rules.explanation: 'Si on allait au restaurant ce soir?' (How about going to a restaurant tonight? / What if we went to a restaurant tonight?).

grammar_rules.title: Formation of the futur simple and irregular stems
grammar_rules.summary: Infinitive (or irregular future stem) + endings: -ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont.
grammar_rules.explanation:
For regular -er and -ir verbs, use the full infinitive. For -re verbs, drop the final 'e'.
Key irregular stems:
- avoir -> aur-
- être -> ser-
- aller -> ir-
- faire -> fer-
- venir -> viendr-
- pouvoir -> pourr-
- vouloir -> voudr-
- savoir -> saur-
- devoir -> devr-
- voir -> verr-
- envoyer -> enverr-

steps: Take infinitive or irregular future stem

notes: The future endings are derived from the present tense of avoir (-ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont).

common_mistakes.explanation: Future 1st person singular ends in -ai, conditional ends in -ais.

grammar_rules.title: The futur antérieur (future perfect)
grammar_rules.summary: Future of auxiliary (aurai/serai) + past participle. Expresses an action that will be completed before another future action.
grammar_rules.explanation: 'Quand j'aurai fini mes études, je trouverai un travail' (When I have finished my studies, I will find a job).

steps: Conjugate avoir or être in futur simple

usage_conditions: Action completed before another future event

grammar_rules.title: Use of future tenses after temporal conjunctions (quand, dès que, etc.)
grammar_rules.summary: French requires the FUTURE tense after quand, lorsque, dès que, aussitôt que, tant que when referring to future events, unlike English which uses present.
grammar_rules.explanation: In English: 'When I arrive, I will call you' (present arrive). In French: 'Quand j'arriverai, je t'appellerai' (future arriverai).
usage_conditions: Time clauses referring to the future

common_mistakes.wrong: Quand j'arrive demain, je te verrai
common_mistakes.correct: Quand j'arriverai demain, je te verrai
common_mistakes.explanation: Use future tense after quand for future time.

grammar_rules.title: Formation of the plus-que-parfait (pluperfect)
grammar_rules.summary: Imparfait of auxiliary (avais/étais) + past participle.
grammar_rules.explanation: Formed with the imparfait of avoir or être followed by the past participle: 'J'avais parlé', 'Elle était partie'. Agreement rules mirror the passé composé.

steps: Conjugate avoir/être in imparfait (avais, avais, avait, avions, aviez, avaient / étais, étais, était, étions, étiez, étaient)

usage_conditions: Actions that took place prior to another past action

grammar_rules.title: Uses of the plus-que-parfait and Si seulement
grammar_rules.summary: 1. Prior past action. 2. Regret with 'Si seulement' (If only...). 3. Past conditional clause (Si + plus-que-parfait).
grammar_rules.explanation:
- Prior past: 'Il avait déjà mangé quand je suis arrivé' (He had already eaten when I arrived).
- Regret: 'Si seulement j'avais su!' (If only I had known!).

grammar_rules.title: Formation and uses of the present conditional
grammar_rules.summary: Future stem + imparfait endings (-ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient). Used for politeness, wishes, and hypothetical actions.
grammar_rules.explanation: Take the future stem (parler-, finir-, vendr-, aur-, ser-, fer-, etc.) and add the imparfait endings: 'Je parlerais', 'Nous aimerions', 'Vous voudriez'. Expresses polite requests, advice, and potential outcomes.

common_mistakes.wrong: Si j'aurais (never use conditional right after si)
common_mistakes.explanation: Never use the conditional directly after 'si'.

grammar_rules.title: Hypothetical sentences with Si + imparfait -> conditionnel présent
grammar_rules.summary: Si + imparfait expresses the condition; the result clause uses the present conditional.
grammar_rules.explanation: 'Si j'avais le temps, je voyagerais dans le monde entier' (If I had time, I would travel around the whole world).
restrictions: Never use the conditional in the si-clause itself.

common_mistakes.explanation: Si takes imparfait, not conditional.

grammar_rules.title: Formation of the past conditional and expressing regrets
grammar_rules.summary: Conditional of auxiliary (aurais/serais) + past participle. Expresses unfulfilled actions and past regrets.
grammar_rules.explanation: Formed with the present conditional of avoir or être followed by the past participle: 'J'aurais aimé vous voir' (I would have liked to see you); 'Elle serait venue' (She would have come).

grammar_rules.title: Translating 'could' into French
grammar_rules.summary: Could = 1. Pourriez-vous (polite request); 2. Pouvais (past general ability); 3. Ai pu (managed to do on a specific occasion); 4. Pourrais (hypothetical).
grammar_rules.explanation:
- Polite request: 'Pourriez-vous m'aider?' (Could you help me?)
- Past general ability: 'Je pouvais courir vite' (I could / was able to run fast)
- Specific past success: 'J'ai pu ouvrir la porte' (I could / managed to open the door)
- Hypothetical: 'Tu pourrais essayer' (You could try).

grammar_rules.title: Translating 'should' into French
grammar_rules.summary: Should (present) = devoir in conditionnel présent (devrais/devrait); Should have (past) = devoir in conditionnel passé (aurais dû).
grammar_rules.explanation:
- Present advice / should: 'Tu devrais te reposer' (You should rest).
- Past regret / should have: 'Tu aurais dû m'appeler' (You should have called me).

grammar_rules.title: Translating 'would' into French
grammar_rules.summary: 1. Hypothetical = Conditionnel (I would go -> J'irais); 2. Habitual past = Imparfait (We would swim every day -> Nous nagions tous les jours); 3. Willingness = Vouloir (Would you please -> Voudriez-vous).
grammar_rules.explanation:
Distinguish between:
- Conditional action: 'Je voyagerais si j'avais l'argent'
- Habit in the past: 'En été, nous allions à la plage' (In summer, we would go to the beach)
- Polite willingness: 'Voudriez-vous fermer la fenêtre?' (Would you close the window?).

common_mistakes.wrong: Chaque jour nous voudrions aller... (for habit)
common_mistakes.explanation: Use imparfait for past habitual 'would'.

grammar_rules.title: Formation of the present subjunctive and irregular stems
grammar_rules.summary: Stem of 3rd person plural present (ils) + -e, -es, -e, -ions, -iez, -ent.
grammar_rules.explanation:
Find the stem from ils/elles present (ils parl-ent, ils finiss-ent, ils vend-ent). Add endings: que je -e, que tu -es, qu'il -e, que nous -ions, que vous -iez, qu'ils -ent.
Irregular stems:
- être: sois, sois, soit, soyons, soyez, soient
- avoir: aie, aies, ait, ayons, ayez, aient
- faire: fass-
- aller: aill- / all-
- pouvoir: puiss-
- savoir: sach-
- vouloir: veuill- / voul-

steps: Nous and vous use 'nous' present stem for stem-changing verbs

exceptions: être, avoir, faire, aller, pouvoir, savoir, vouloir are irregular

common_mistakes.explanation: Faire uses stem fass- in subjunctive.

grammar_rules.title: Subjunctive after verbs of necessity, will, and desire
grammar_rules.summary: Use subjunctive after il faut que, vouloir que, désirer que, exiger que, demander que.
grammar_rules.explanation: When two different subjects are involved and the main clause expresses a command, wish, or necessity: 'Il faut que tu viennes' (You must come); 'Je veux qu'elle parte' (I want her to leave).
usage_conditions: Two different subjects with expressing will/necessity
exceptions: Espérer que takes indicative (J'espère qu'il viendra), not subjunctive.

common_mistakes.explanation: Espérer takes the indicative mood.

grammar_rules.title: Conjunctions that always require the subjunctive
grammar_rules.summary: bien que, quoique (although), pour que, afin que (so that), avant que (before), sans que (without), à condition que (on condition that), pourvu que (provided that), jusqu'à ce que (until).
grammar_rules.explanation:
These conjunctions introduce clauses expressing concession, purpose, condition, or anticipation and always trigger the subjunctive:
- 'Bien qu'il pleuve, nous sortirons' (Although it's raining, we will go out).
- 'Je t'explique pour que tu comprennes' (I'm explaining so that you understand).
usage_conditions: Subordinate clauses with special adverbial conjunctions
exceptions: après que takes indicative, though spoken French often confuses it.

common_mistakes.explanation: Bien que always requires the subjunctive.

grammar_rules.title: Uses of the present infinitive: after prepositions and as subject
grammar_rules.summary: In French, all prepositions (pour, sans, avant de, afin de, à, de) take the infinitive (never the -ing form as in English).
grammar_rules.explanation: Unlike English which uses the gerund (-ing) after prepositions ('without knowing', 'before leaving'), French requires the infinitive: 'sans savoir', 'avant de partir', 'pour réussir'.
usage_conditions: After prepositions (except 'en' which takes the gerund)
exceptions: 'en' takes the present participle / gerund (en mangeant).

common_mistakes.explanation: Use avant de + infinitive.

grammar_rules.title: The past infinitive with après (après avoir / après être)
grammar_rules.summary: 'Après' is ALWAYS followed by the past infinitive (après avoir fait, après être parti).
grammar_rules.explanation: To express 'after doing something', French uses après + past infinitive: 'Après avoir dîné, nous sommes allés au cinéma' (After having dinner / After dining, we went to the movies).
usage_conditions: Actions completed prior to the main clause action

common_mistakes.explanation: Après requires the past infinitive.

grammar_rules.title: Verbs followed by à + infinitive
grammar_rules.summary: Key verbs taking à before an infinitive: commencer à, apprendre à, inviter à, réussir à, hésiter à, continuer à, aider à.
grammar_rules.explanation:
- commencer à parler
- apprendre à conduire
- réussir à finir
- hésiter à répondre
- aider quelqu'un à faire quelque chose

grammar_rules.title: Verbs followed by de + infinitive
grammar_rules.summary: Key verbs taking de before an infinitive: accepter de, refuser de, décider de, demander de, essayer de, oublier de, promettre de, regretter de, risquer de.
grammar_rules.explanation:
- décider de partir
- demander de venir
- essayer de comprendre
- oublier de téléphoner
- refuser de parler

grammar_rules.title: Verbs followed directly by an infinitive without preposition
grammar_rules.summary: Semi-auxiliary and modal verbs followed directly by an infinitive (no preposition): aimer, aller, devoir, pouvoir, savoir, vouloir, préférer, espérer, laisser, faire.
grammar_rules.explanation:
- Je veux partir (not je veux de partir)
- Il doit travailler
- Nous aimons voyager
- Elle préfère rester

common_mistakes.explanation: Vouloir takes direct infinitive without preposition.

grammar_rules.title: Formation of the present participle and verbal adjectives
grammar_rules.summary: Drop -ons from the present 'nous' form and add -ant. Irregulars: ayant (avoir), étant (être), sachant (savoir).
grammar_rules.explanation: Verbal adjectives agree in gender and number with the noun they modify (des histoires amusantes), whereas present participles acting as verbs do not agree (une femme parlant français).
exceptions: ayant (avoir), étant (être), sachant (savoir)

grammar_rules.title: The gerund (en + present participle): simultaneity, means, and condition
grammar_rules.summary: Formed with 'en' + present participle. Expresses while doing (simultaneity), by doing (means), or if doing (condition).
grammar_rules.explanation:
1. Simultaneity: 'Il écoute de la musique en travaillant' (He listens to music while working).
2. Means / Manner: 'C'est en forgeant qu'on devient forgeron' (Practice makes perfect / By forging one becomes a blacksmith).
3. 'Tout en' emphasizes simultaneous contrast: 'Tout en souriant, elle refusait' (While still smiling, she refused).
usage_conditions: Both actions must share the same subject
restrictions: Subject of gerund must be identical to subject of main clause.

grammar_rules.title: Formation of the passé simple for regular verbs
grammar_rules.summary: -er verbs take -a endings (-ai, -as, -a, -âmes, -âtes, -èrent); -ir/-re verbs take -i endings (-is, -is, -it, -îmes, -îtes, -irent).
grammar_rules.explanation: The passé simple is the literary past tense used in written French narratives (novels, history, formal journalism). Third person forms (il parla, ils parlèrent / il finit, ils finirent) are by far the most frequent.
usage_conditions: Written literature, formal history, fairy tales
restrictions: Almost never used in spoken conversation.

grammar_rules.title: Irregular passé simple: -u-, -i-, and -in- patterns
grammar_rules.summary: Three irregular vowel patterns: 1. -u- pattern (eut, fut, put, voulut, sut, dut); 2. -i- pattern (vit, prit, mit, dit, fit); 3. -in- pattern (vint, tint).
grammar_rules.explanation:
- Avoir: il eut, ils eurent
- Être: il fut, ils furent
- Faire: il fit, ils firent
- Venir: il vint, ils vinrent
- Voir: il vit, ils virent
- Pouvoir: il put, ils purent

grammar_rules.title: Formation of the passive voice and agent prepositions (par / de)
grammar_rules.summary: Être (in any tense) + past participle (agreeing with subject) + par / de + agent.
grammar_rules.explanation: Active: 'Le chat mange la souris' -> Passive: 'La souris est mangée par le chat'. The past participle always agrees in gender and number with the grammatical subject. 'Par' is standard; 'de' is used with state/emotion verbs (aimé de, respecté de, entouré de).

steps: Conjugate être in the original tense
Add past participle of action verb agreeing with subject

usage_conditions: Emphasizing the result or the recipient of the action

common_mistakes.explanation: Participle agrees with feminine subject 'la maison'.

grammar_rules.title: Avoiding the passive voice in French using 'on' or pronominal verbs
grammar_rules.summary: French prefers active sentences using 'on' (On parle français) or passive pronominals (Le français se parle) over literal passive constructions.
grammar_rules.explanation:
Instead of 'Le pont a été détruit', French frequently prefers:
1. Active with 'on': 'On a détruit le pont'.
2. Passive pronominal: 'Ce livre se lit facilement'.

grammar_rules.title: Reporting statements and questions in indirect speech
grammar_rules.summary: Reporting verbs take 'que' for statements, 'si' for yes/no questions, 'ce que' for qu'est-ce que, and 'de + infinitive' for commands.
grammar_rules.explanation:
- Statements: Il dit : « Je pars » -> Il dit qu'il part.
- Yes/No questions: Il demande : « Est-ce que tu viens ? » -> Il demande si je viens.
- What questions: Il demande : « Qu'est-ce que tu fais ? » -> Il demande ce que je fais.
- Commands: Il dit : « Partez ! » -> Il dit de partir.

common_mistakes.wrong: Il demande qu'est-ce que je fais
common_mistakes.correct: Il demande ce que je fais
common_mistakes.explanation: Qu'est-ce que changes to 'ce que' in indirect speech.

grammar_rules.title: Tense shifts in indirect speech (la concordance des temps)
grammar_rules.summary: When reporting verb is in the past: Present -> Imparfait; Passé composé -> Plus-que-parfait; Futur simple -> Conditionnel présent.
grammar_rules.explanation:
If the introductory verb is in a past tense (il a dit, il disait):
- Présent becomes Imparfait: 'Je suis fatigué' -> Il a dit qu'il était fatigué.
- Passé composé becomes Plus-que-parfait: 'J'ai fini' -> Il a dit qu'il avait fini.
- Futur simple becomes Conditionnel présent: 'Je viendrai' -> Il a dit qu'il viendrait.
usage_conditions: Indirect speech introduced by a past tense verb
exceptions: If the introductory verb is in the present (il dit), tenses do NOT shift.

common_mistakes.wrong: Il a dit qu'il viendra demain
common_mistakes.correct: Il a dit qu'il viendrait le lendemain
common_mistakes.explanation: Future shifts to conditional when introductory verb is in past.

grammar_rules.title: Formation of the imperative and dropping 's' in the tu form
grammar_rules.summary: Three forms: tu, nous, vous without subject pronouns. Drop the final 's' in the 'tu' form of -er verbs and aller (Parle!, Va!), except before y or en (Vas-y!, Manges-en!).
grammar_rules.explanation:
Regular -er verbs and aller drop the final -s in the tu form: 'Parle!', 'Écoute!', 'Va!'. However, when followed by y or en, the -s is kept for liaison: 'Vas-y!', 'Manges-en!'.
Irregular imperative stems:
- être: sois, soyons, soyez
- avoir: aie, ayons, ayez
- savoir: sache, sachons, sachez
- vouloir: veuillez

steps: Use tu, nous, vous present forms without pronouns
Drop 's' in tu form for -er verbs and aller

exceptions: être (sois/soyons/soyez), avoir (aie/ayons/ayez), savoir (sache/sachons/sachez), vouloir (veuillez)

common_mistakes.correct: Parle! / Va! (unless followed by y/en: Vas-y!)
common_mistakes.explanation: Drop 's' in tu command for -er verbs.

grammar_rules.title: Pronominal verbs in affirmative vs negative imperative
grammar_rules.summary: Affirmative: verb-toi / verb-nous / verb-vous (Lève-toi!). Negative: ne te/nous/vous verb pas (Ne te lève pas!).
grammar_rules.explanation:
- Affirmative: Pronoun follows with a hyphen; 'te' becomes 'toi': 'Habille-toi!', 'Asseyons-nous!', 'Dépêchez-vous!'.
- Negative: Pronoun precedes the verb; 'te' remains 'te': 'Ne t'habille pas!', 'Ne nous asseyons pas!', 'Ne vous dépêchez pas!'.
usage_conditions: Commands with reflexive or reciprocal verbs

common_mistakes.explanation: Use 'te' before verb in negative command.

grammar_rules.title: Definite articles and contractions with à and de
grammar_rules.summary: le, la, l', les. Contractions: à + le = au, à + les = aux; de + le = du, de + les = des.
grammar_rules.explanation:
Definite articles designate specific items or general concepts in French (L'amour, La liberté). When combined with à or de, le and les contract:
- à + le -> au (au cinéma)
- à + les -> aux (aux étudiants)
- de + le -> du (du professeur)
- de + les -> des (des enfants)
exceptions: No contraction with 'la' or 'l'' (à la maison, de l'eau).

common_mistakes.explanation: à + le must contract to au.

grammar_rules.title: Country gender and prepositions (en, au, aux, à)
grammar_rules.summary: Countries ending in -e are feminine (use 'en': en France, en Italie). Masculine countries use 'au' (au Canada, au Japon). Plural countries use 'aux' (aux États-Unis). Cities use 'à' (à Paris).
grammar_rules.explanation:
- Feminine country / vowel start: 'en' (en France, en Espagne, en Iran)
- Masculine country starting with consonant: 'au' (au Mexique, au Canada, au Japon)
- Plural countries: 'aux' (aux États-Unis, aux Pays-Bas)
- Cities: 'à' (à Paris, à Tokyo, à New York)
- Coming from: de/d' (fem: de France), du (masc: du Canada), des (pl: des États-Unis), de (cities: de Paris).
usage_conditions: Expressing destination (to/in) or origin (from) with geographical places
exceptions: Le Mexique, le Mozambique, le Cambodge, le Zimbabwe end in -e but are masculine (au Mexique).

common_mistakes.explanation: Use 'en' for feminine countries.

grammar_rules.title: Direct object pronouns (me, te, le, la, nous, vous, les)
grammar_rules.summary: Replace a direct object noun (answering what? or whom?). Placed before the conjugated verb (or before the infinitive).
grammar_rules.explanation:
- Je vois le film -> Je le vois.
- Il aime cette chanson -> Il l'aime.
- Nous invitons les amis -> Nous les invitons.
With an infinitive: 'Je veux le voir' (placed before the infinitive it belongs to).

common_mistakes.explanation: Use direct object pronoun le/la before the verb.

grammar_rules.title: Indirect object pronouns (me, te, lui, nous, vous, leur)
grammar_rules.summary: Replace 'à + person'. 'Lui' = to him/her (singular); 'Leur' = to them (plural).
grammar_rules.explanation:
Used with verbs that take 'à + person' (parler à, téléphoner à, demander à, écrire à, répondre à, donner à):
- Je parle à Pierre -> Je lui parle.
- Je parle à Marie -> Je lui parle (lui is both masc and fem!).
- J'écris aux parents -> Je leur écris (never 'leurs'!).
notes: 'Lui' is used for both masculine and feminine singular. 'Leur' never takes an -s as a pronoun.

common_mistakes.explanation: The pronoun leur never takes an s.

grammar_rules.title: Order of double object pronouns before the verb
grammar_rules.summary: Order before verb: 1. (me, te, se, nous, vous) -> 2. (le, la, les) -> 3. (lui, leur) -> 4. y -> 5. en.
grammar_rules.explanation:
Example combinations:
- 'Il me le donne' (1 + 2)
- 'Je le lui donne' (2 + 3)
- 'Il lui en parle' (3 + 5)
- 'Je vous y emmène' (1 + 4)
- 'Il y en a' (4 + 5)
exceptions: In affirmative imperative, order changes: [VERB] - le/la/les - moi/toi/lui/nous/vous/leur - y - en (Donne-le-moi!).

common_mistakes.explanation: Direct (le) precedes 3rd person indirect (lui).

grammar_rules.title: Adjective agreement in gender and number
grammar_rules.summary: Adjectives agree in gender (+e for fem) and number (+s for plural) with the noun they modify.
grammar_rules.explanation:
Special masculine forms before vowel/silent h: beau -> bel, nouveau -> nouvel, vieux -> vieil.
Feminine forms: belle, nouvelle, vieille.
exceptions: Compound color adjectives (bleu marine, vert clair) and invariable colors (marron, orange) do not agree.

common_mistakes.explanation: Use bel before masculine noun starting with vowel.

grammar_rules.title: Placement of adjectives: the BAGS rule (Beauty, Age, Goodness, Size)
grammar_rules.summary: Most adjectives follow the noun in French, except BAGS adjectives which precede the noun.
grammar_rules.explanation:
- Beauty: beau, joli
- Age: jeune, vieux, nouveau
- Goodness: bon, mauvais, meilleur, gentil
- Size: grand, petit, gros, haut, long
Example: 'une jolie maison', 'un vieux livre', 'une grande ville'.
notes: Some adjectives change meaning based on position: grand homme (great man) vs homme grand (tall man); pauvre homme (pitiful) vs homme pauvre (poor).

common_mistakes.explanation: BAGS adjectives precede the noun.

grammar_rules.title: Demonstrative adjectives (ce, cet, cette, ces)
grammar_rules.summary: ce (masc. cons), cet (masc. vowel/silent h), cette (fem), ces (plural).
grammar_rules.explanation:
- ce livre (this/that book)
- cet hôtel / cet homme (before vowel/silent h)
- cette table (this/that table)
- ces livres / ces tables (these/those books/tables)
Add -ci (this) or -là (that) to emphasize proximity: 'ce livre-ci', 'ce livre-là'.

common_mistakes.explanation: Use cet before masculine noun beginning with vowel or silent h.

grammar_rules.title: Demonstrative pronouns (celui, celle, ceux, celles)
grammar_rules.summary: Replace demonstrative adjective + noun: celui (m.sg), celle (f.sg), ceux (m.pl), celles (f.pl).
grammar_rules.explanation:
Demonstrative pronouns cannot stand alone; they must be followed by:
1. -ci or -là: 'celui-ci', 'celle-là'
2. 'de' + possessor: 'celui de Pierre' (Pierre's one)
3. A relative pronoun (qui, que, dont): 'celui qui parle' (the one who is speaking).
usage_conditions: Replacing a specific noun previously mentioned
restrictions: Never used alone without -ci/-là, de, or relative clause.

grammar_rules.title: Relative pronouns: Qui (subject) versus Que (direct object)
grammar_rules.summary: 'Qui' is followed by a verb (subject). 'Que' (or qu') is followed by a subject + verb (direct object).
grammar_rules.explanation:
- Qui: 'L'homme qui parle' (The man who is speaking - qui is the subject of parle).
- Que: 'Le livre que je lis' (The book that I am reading - je is subject, que is direct object).
Note: 'qui' never elides to qu', only 'que' elides to 'qu'' before a vowel.

common_mistakes.explanation: Qui never elides before a vowel.

grammar_rules.title: The relative pronoun dont (replacing de + noun)
grammar_rules.summary: 'Dont' replaces 'de + noun' (expressing of which, whose, about which).
grammar_rules.explanation:
Used whenever the verb, adjective, or noun in the relative clause takes 'de':
- parler de -> 'Le film dont je parle'
- avoir besoin de -> 'Ce dont j'ai besoin'
- être fier de -> 'L'enfant dont il est fier'
- possession (whose) -> 'L'auteur dont j'ai lu le livre'.
notes: Do not repeat 'de' or possessive after dont: 'L'homme dont le fils est médecin' (not 'dont son fils').

common_mistakes.explanation: Use definite article, not possessive, with dont.

grammar_rules.title: Placement of adverbs of frequency and time
grammar_rules.summary: Short adverbs of frequency (souvent, toujours, jamais, bien, mal) immediately follow the conjugated verb; in compound tenses they sit between auxiliary and past participle.
grammar_rules.explanation:
- Simple tense: 'Il parle souvent français' (after verb).
- Compound tense: 'Il a souvent parlé français' (between auxiliary and participle).
- Time expressions (hier, demain, ce matin) usually sit at beginning or end of sentence.

common_mistakes.explanation: Adverbs follow conjugated verb in French.

grammar_rules.title: Interrogative question words (Où, Quand, Comment, Pourquoi, Combien)
grammar_rules.summary: Où (where), Quand (when), Comment (how), Pourquoi (why), Combien (how much/many), Qui (who), Que/Qu' (what).
grammar_rules.explanation:
Combined with est-ce que or inversion:
- 'Où habitez-vous?' / 'Où est-ce que vous habitez?'
- 'Pourquoi pars-tu?' / 'Pourquoi est-ce que tu pars?'

grammar_rules.title: Cardinal and ordinal numbers in French
grammar_rules.summary: Ordinals: premier/première, deuxième, troisième, etc. (add -ième to cardinal number).
grammar_rules.explanation: Dates use cardinal numbers in French, except for the first of the month which uses 'premier': 'le premier mai' vs 'le deux mai'.
exceptions: un -> premier/première; cinq -> cinquième; neuf -> neuvième

common_mistakes.explanation: Only the 1st of the month uses ordinal premier.

grammar_rules.title: French counting system for 70, 80, and 90
grammar_rules.summary: 70 = soixante-dix; 71 = soixante et onze; 80 = quatre-vingts; 81 = quatre-vingt-un; 90 = quatre-vingt-dix; 91 = quatre-vingt-onze.
grammar_rules.explanation:
- 70s: soixante-dix, soixante et onze, soixante-douze...
- 80s: quatre-vingts (note the 's' on vingt only when not followed by another number), quatre-vingt-un...
- 90s: quatre-vingt-dix, quatre-vingt-onze, quatre-vingt-douze...
- 'mille' is invariable (deux mille, never milles).

common_mistakes.explanation: Drop the 's' on quatre-vingts when another number follows.

grammar_rules.title: Verbs with different prepositions carrying different meanings
grammar_rules.summary: penser à (think about) vs penser de (have an opinion on); manquer à (miss someone) vs manquer de (lack); jouer à (sports/games) vs jouer de (musical instruments).
grammar_rules.explanation:
- Penser à: 'Je pense à mes vacances' (Thinking about)
- Penser de: 'Que pensez-vous de ce film?' (What is your opinion of...)
- Manquer de: 'Il manque d'argent' (He lacks money)
- Manquer à: 'Tu me manques' (You are missing to me = I miss you)
- Jouer à: 'jouer au tennis', 'jouer aux échecs'
- Jouer de: 'jouer du piano', 'jouer de la guitare'.

common_mistakes.wrong: Tu me manques (misunderstood as you miss me)
common_mistakes.correct: Tu me manques = I miss you (literally: you are missing to me)
common_mistakes.explanation: The person missed is the subject.

grammar_rules.title: Indefinite n'importe expressions and Avoir beau + infinitive
grammar_rules.summary: 1. n'importe quoi (whatever), n'importe qui (whoever), n'importe où (wherever), n'importe quand (whenever). 2. avoir beau + infinitive = however much one tries / in vain.
grammar_rules.explanation:
- 'J'ai beau chercher, je ne trouve pas mes clés' (No matter how much I look / Even though I look everywhere, I can't find my keys).
- 'Quitte à' = even if it means / at the risk of: 'Quitte à rater mon train, je dois lui parler'.

steps: Conjugate avoir + beau + infinitive of action verb

The present indicative is used in a number of ways: ◆ To make a general statement and to describe ongoing actions in the present. It can be translated in three different ways. One more use of the present tense: depuis The present tense is used to express an action that began in the past and continues in the present. Note that in English, the past tense is used. There are different ways to formulate the questions, using either depuis, il y a... que, cela (ça) fait... que. Let's start with depuis. To ask a question about the duration of an action, use depuis quand (since when) or depuis combien de temps (how long). We are waiting for an answer. The interrogative form In French there are three ways of asking questions. You can do an inversion of the subject and the verb, use the est-ce que form, or simply use the affirmative form with an upward intonation. Let's start with the inversion: Comprenez-vous la question? Do you understand the question? Parlez-vous espagnol? Do you speak Spanish? If the third-person singular of a verb ends with a vowel, a -t- is inserted to facilitate the pronunciation. Parle-t-elle russe? Does she speak Russian? Voyage-t-il souvent en Europe? Does he often travel to Europe? A more colloquial way of asking a question is to use the est-ce que form in front of the subject  verb. Est-ce que vous habitez à New York? Do you live in New York? Est-ce que tu sors ce soir? Are you going out tonight? Est-ce que becomes est-ce qu' before a vowel. Est-ce que vous courez dans le parc? Do you run in the park? Est-ce qu'ils vendent des timbres? Do they sell stamps? A third way of asking a question, colloquially, is keeping the order subject  verb and speaking with an upward intonation. Tu finis à cinq heures? You're finishing at five o'clock? Il (pleuvoir) demain. As in English, the French future tense is used to describe future events. Les étudiants passeront leurs examens Students will take their exams in May. en mai. Les cours recommenceront en décembre. Courses will resume in December. In a compound sentence in French, if the main clause is in the futur simple, the dependent clause, introduced by some conjunctions, will also be in the futur simple. Note that in English, such a dependent clause will be in the present tense. aussitôt que as soon as dès que as soon as lorsque when quand when tant que as long as Elle ira à Paris quand elle aura le temps. She'll go to Paris when she has time. Il nous dira lorsqu'il faudra parler. He'll tell us when we have to talk. Elle vous préviendra dès qu'elle aura She'll inform you as soon as she gets the results. les résultats. Aussitôt qu'il arrivera, nous partirons. As soon as he arrives, we'll leave. Elle vous téléphonera aussitôt qu'elle She'll call you as soon as she lands in London. atterrira à Londres. Tant qu'il y aura du soleil, nous As long as the sun is out, we'll stay on the terrace. resterons sur la terrasse. The future tense of être and avoir is sometimes used to express probability in the present, to indicate something that is likely or allegedly true. The futur simple and the futur antérieur 75 L'étudiant n'est pas en classe. Il sera The student is not in class. He is probably encore endormi. still asleep. Le professeur n'a pas demandé nos The teacher did not ask for our homework. devoirs. Il sera distrait. He's probably distracted. In a narration, the futur simple can be used to express a future idea from the standpoint of the past, as shown in the following examples. (Note that English uses a conditional form, would, in this case.) Malheureusement, ses œuvres ne seront Unfortunately, her works would become reconnues qu'après sa mort. recognized only after her death. Un des génies du dix-huitième siècle et il One of the geniuses of the eighteenth mourra dans la misère. century, and he would die in misery. The futur simple can be used instead of an imperative (command form) to achieve a less peremptory tone. Vous voudrez bien lui envoyer ma réponse. Please send him my answer. Some verbs are not followed by a preposition, others are followed by à, de, sur, etc., before an infinitive, and sometimes before a noun or pronoun. Les élèves sont punis par le professeur. The passive voice 139 The agent with par and with de in the passive voice In most cases, the agent is introduced by par. Ce rapport a été fait par un consultant This report was written by an American américain. consultant. Cette bague a été retrouvée par la police. This ring was found by the police. Ce manoir a été construit par une This mansion was built by a wealthy family. famille fortunée. Ces éditoriaux seront écrits par notre These editorials will be written by our rédacteur en chef. editor in chief. However, the preposition de is commonly used after verbs expressing emotion or opinion. Ce professeur est apprécié de ses This teacher is appreciated by his students. étudiants. Ce gérant est estimé de ses employés. This manager is respected by his employees. That is, when the voix passive is followed by the preposition de (rather than par), the agent plays a less active role. Le voleur est suivi de ses complices. The thief is followed by his accomplices. Le voleur est suivi par la police. The thief is followed by the police. Le château est entouré de douves. The castle is surrounded by a moat. Le château est entouré par les The castle is surrounded by the invaders. envahisseurs. Uses of the passive voice The voix passive is used to emphasize the subject. Une écharpe blanche a été retrouvée sur A white scarf was found on the crime scene. les lieux du crime. Le témoignage de M. Baulieu a été Mr. Baulieu's testimony was heard this entendu ce matin. morning. The voix passive is also used to avoid specifying the agent of the action. Aucune décision ne sera prise avant No decision will be made before the new l'arrivée du nouveau directeur. director's arrival. Son incompétence a été très remarquée. His incompetence was clearly noticed. Aucun rapport n'a été envoyé. No report was sent. Avoiding the passive voice in French The voix passive can be replaced by the active voice in French with the following reflexive verbs: se laisser, se faire, se voir, s'entendre dire. Note the passive voice forms in the English translations. Elle s'est fait faire un robe pour son She had a dress made for her wedding. mariage. Il s'est vu contraint d'accepter. Do you know her? Indirect object pronouns Now that you have mastered the pronom objet direct, let's take a look at the pronom objet indirect (indirect object pronoun). In English there are five indirect object pronouns me, you, him, her, us. As always, French distinguishes between an informal you (te) and a formal or plural you (vous). The French indirect object pronoun does not, however, distinguish gender; lui and leur replace both masculine and feminine nouns. In French, the indirect object pronoun replaces only animate indirect objects (people, animals). Inanimate ideas and things are replaced with the indirect object pronouns y and en, which will be discussed later in this chapter. Let's look at the indirect object pronouns: SINGULAR PLURAL me (m') me nous us te (t') you (familiar) vous you (formal or plural) lui him, her leur them (masc. and fem.) The object is called indirect when the verb is controlled by a preposition (parler à, répondre à, écrire à, etc.). The indirect object pronoun is placed before the conjugated verb and before avoir in the compound tenses. Although the past participle agrees in gender and number with the preceding direct object, the past participle never agrees with an indirect object pronoun. The All the pronouns 171 indirect object pronouns me and te become m' and t' before vowels and mute h. Make sure to distinguish between leur, the indirect object pronoun, and leur(s), the possessive adjective. Tu parles au journaliste. You are talking to the journalist. Tu lui parles. You are talking to him. Tu réponds à Andrée. You answer Andrée. Tu lui réponds. You answer her. Vous écrivez à l'agent. You write to the agent. Vous lui écrivez. You write to him. Vous expliquez la situation aux clients. You explain the situation to the customers. Vous leur expliquez la situation. You explain the situation to them. Elle nous enverra une confirmation. She'll send us a confirmation. Je vous donnerai un jour de congé. I'll give you a day off. Il me rendra le livre demain. He'll return the book to me tomorrow. Ils t'apporteront des fleurs. They'll bring you some flowers. In the interrogative or negative, the indirect object pronoun is placed immediately before the verb. Lui as-tu parlé de ce livre? Did you talk to him about this book? M'avez-vous envoyé un courriel? Did you send me an e-mail? Vous fournit-il de bons produits? Does he provide you with good products? Leur avez-vous envoyé les révisions? Did you send them the revisions? Elle ne nous envoie jamais rien. She never sends us anything. Tu ne m'apportes que des mauvaises You only bring me bad news. nouvelles. Vous ne lui avez pas dit la vérité. You did not tell him the truth. Ils te prêteront leur voiture. They'll lend you their car. Indirect object pronouns in the imperative In the affirmative imperative, the indirect object pronoun follows the verb. Me (m') and te (t') become moi and toi. Remember to link the verb to the following pronoun with a hyphen. In the negative imperative, the indirect object pronoun remains before the verb. Téléphone-moi demain matin! Call me tomorrow morning! Prêtez-lui votre dictionnaire! Lend him your dictionary! Apportez-nous de nouveaux accessoires! Bring us new props! Envoyez-leur le script! Send them the script! Ne lui donnez rien! Don't give him anything! Ne nous téléphonez pas si tard! Don't call us so late!

INDIRECT OBJECT DIRECT OBJECT me (m') te (t')   le, la, l', les nous vous Elle te donne le rôle. She gives you the part. Elle te le donne. She gives it to you. Nous vous envoyons le contrat. Il m'offre la bague de sa mère. He gives me his mother's ring. Il me l'offre. He gives it to me. If the direct and indirect pronouns in the third person are combined, the direct object pronoun comes first. DIRECT OBJECT INDIRECT OBJECT le (l') la (l')   lui, leur les J'envoie la lettre au rédacteur. I send the letter to the editor. Je la lui envoie. I send it to him. Elle tend le document au médecin. Comparatives and superlatives Comparison of adjectives and adverbs In French, comparisons of adjectives and adverbs can take three forms, plus... que (more . . . than), moins... que (less . . . than), aussi... que (as . . . as). For example: Ce modèle est plus récent que le mien. This model is more recent than mine. New York est plus grand que San Francisco. New York is bigger than San Francisco. Marc est moins riche que Paul. Mark is less rich than Paul. Luc est aussi célèbre que Bertrand. Luc is as famous as Bertrand. Comparison of nouns To compare quantities, use the following expressions. Note the use of de (d') with expressions of quantity: Elle a plus de temps que Valérie. She has more time than Valérie. Il a moins de chance que toi. He is less lucky than you are. Elle a autant de jouets que toi. She has as many toys as you do. Irregular comparatives Some comparatives have irregular forms. Ce livre est bon. This book is good. Ce livre-ci est meilleur que ce livre-là. This book is better than that book. Il se porte bien. He's feeling well. Il se porte mieux qu'avant. He is feeling better than before. La situation économique est mauvaise. The economic situation is bad. La situation économique est pire qu'avant. The economic situation is worse than before. Cela n'a pas le moindre intérêt. That does not have the slightest interest. Superlatives To express the ideas of the most, the least, the best, the worst, etc., one uses the superlative. To form the superlative in French, simply precede the comparative form by the definite article. Note that before naming a group or entity, the superlative is followed by de  the definite article. 188 practice makes perfect Complete French Grammar C'est le plus grand spectacle du monde. It's the greatest show on earth. C'est la plus belle histoire que j'aie jamais lue. It's the most beautiful story I ever read. Adverbs and expressions of time, frequency, and location 217 218 practice makes perfect Complete French Grammar Je voyage souvent en Italie. I often travel in Italy. J'ai souvent voyagé en Italie. I often traveled in Italy. Vous mentez rarement. You rarely lie. Vous avez rarement menti. You have rarely lied. To express time with the passé composé, pendant (for, during) is commonly used (although it can actually be omitted). However, pour (for) is never used to talk about duration in the past. questions.prompt: Le patron a manqué à ses devoirs. Whatever, whenever, wherever, whoever The present subjunctive is used with the indefinite expressions that are the French equivalents of whatever, whenever, wherever, and whoever. When the English whatever is followed by subject  verb, use the neuter quoi que  present subjunctive. Quoi que tu fasses, je t'aimerai toujours. Whatever you do, I will always love you. Quoi qu'elle dise, je ne changerai pas Whatever she says, I will not change my mind. d'avis. When the English whatever is followed by a noun, use quel que (quelle que, quels que, quelles que)  the subjunctive of être  noun. Quel que agrees in gender and number with the noun that follows it. Quel que soit votre conseil, je prendrai Whatever your advice, I will make an rendez-vous avec le patron. appointment with the boss. Quelle que soit leur décision, elle Whatever their decision, she will resign. démissionnera. Look at the following examples that express wherever (où que) in French: Où que tu sois, appelle-moi. Wherever you are, call me. Où qu'elle aille, il ira aussi. Wherever she goes, he will go, too. The subjunctive is also used following the expression of whoever (qui que). For example: Qui que tu sois, tu peux lui parler. Whoever you are, you can talk to him. Qui que vous soyez, ouvrez votre cœur. Whoever you are, open up your heart.
